prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single B006 part with Autor, Hanson and Katz. I re-tested it against the chair's questions. First, my round-1 text said B034 was ranked lower by several colleagues. That is a support count, not an argument about merit, and I withdraw it. The substantive reason I place B006 above B034 is narrower. In B006 the framework and the evidence can be audited against each other. The skill-demand and task account says what labour-demand shifts should look like. The local-labour-market designs for import competition test the trade side against regional and micro data, and those designs have been re-examined by other researchers for over a decade. B034 is mature and transparent and I still value it highly, but its scientific consequence runs mainly through applications of a toolkit. On the chair's question about what changed my mind: it was the attribution and checkability comparison, and not the number of first-place votes. I cannot fully rule out that reading colleagues' openings shaped how I framed it. My opening already ranked B006 third and B034 first, and what moved me was that colleagues' attribution and maturity arguments for B004 and B007 did not displace B006. On Katz versus Dorn, I keep Katz because the citation covers how technology and trade shift labour demand, and the long-run skill-premium and wage-structure work supplies the demand-side account that the trade-shock evidence plugs into. My preference order within B006 is Autor-Hanson-Katz, then Autor-Dorn-Hanson, then Autor-Hanson. The citation avoids claiming origination of the task framework, avoids a settled long-run magnitude for the China shock, and does not restate the 2023 or 2024 citations. I read the persistence and shift-share debate as bearing on how large and how lasting the effects are, not on whether they exist. The wording on adjustment and labour demand reflects what has been shown.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem has not been solved, only made explicit. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is excluded purely by the three-name cap. Levy, Murnane and, on task-model theory, Acemoglu lie outside the credited names. Katz's best-known education-technology work with Goldin overlaps with a recent laureate, so his marginal claim is the most exposed in the trio. Colleagues who have not rejected the technology-versus-trade split as two lines may be right, and a citation spanning both strands risks being a composite and not one discovery. As someone who reads empirical claims with replication in mind, I also hold that shift-share designs carry real inference concerns. The broad finding has survived scrutiny, but the headline magnitudes should not anchor a prize rationale. B007 has cleaner credit, and B004 has larger policy reach. Neither is dismissed on merit alone.

responses.point: Friberg keeps B007 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) first, citing cleaner credit and a unified programme. He ranks B006 sixth and would credit only Autor and Hanson, treating Katz and Dorn as adjacent complications.
responses.response: I take the credit-cleanliness point seriously, and B007 is the strongest option for a clean three-name attribution on the list. Two things keep me from preferring it. First, he names identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects as the main weakness, and that is the dimension I weigh heavily. Second, the evidence base is harder to audit than local-labour-market designs. He also says Besley is a closer call than the other two. On the two-name proposal, the real choice is not two versus three names. If the committee wants the narrow China-shock-and-tasks story, the question is Katz versus Dorn. An Autor-Hanson pair would leave out both Dorn's role in the trade-shock work and Katz's long-run skill-demand strand. I do not think the pair is more defensible on credit, only smaller. I respect that his preference rests on scientific reasoning and not on count, and I do not read it as a credit-and-timing preference alone.

responses.point: Strömberg says Katz's marginal claim is the most exposed in the trio because of the Goldin overlap. He names Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the natural fallback within the same discovery. He also ranks B034 fourth as a methods toolkit and not a discovery in its own right.
responses.response: I agree that the Katz claim is the soft spot, and I accept the fallback as a legitimate configuration. I would separate Katz's wage-structure and skill-premium contribution from the education-technology book with Goldin. The former is what I credit, and the citation wording should say so. On B034, I accept that a methods toolkit has a different kind of reach and I have ranked it as an alternative for that reason. But I would not say it is not a discovery. Demand estimation with endogenous prices and differentiated products changed what can be estimated in antitrust and industry analysis, and the sensitivity to implementation and instruments is well documented and open to replication. It is my first alternative, not a rejected option. I would only prefer it if B006 stalled on credit division.

responses.point: Teorell asks whether B006 is one achievement or two. He says Dorn would be the more precise credit for a trade-shock-only citation, that the Katz strand is the committee's closest call within B006, and that the Goldin and Acemoglu adjacency may weigh on timing.
responses.response: I think one citation can hold both strands if it is framed around labour-demand adjustment, which is the common outcome, and does not claim that technology and trade are one mechanism. The test is whether a reader can name what each of the three contributed to a single question. Autor links the task and trade strands, Hanson anchors the import-competition design, and Katz anchors the long-run skill-demand account. That test is satisfied, though not perfectly. On adjacency, I agree the committee should say what B006 adds to the 2023 and 2024 prizes. My answer is that it adds the direct evidence on trade exposure and local adjustment and the empirical skill-demand account, neither of which was the subject of those citations. I would treat adjacency as a drafting constraint and not as a reason to defer on merit.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B034 second and credits its clean BLP core. He still places B006 ahead on breadth of scientific consequence. He raises how the dynamic-game strand and Bresnahan would be handled in a B034 citation.
responses.response: I agree with the assessment and I appreciate the fair reading of my case. The B034 attribution problem is real beyond the BLP core, because the dynamic-game strand and Bresnahan's contributions would need a drafted line, and a trio of Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn does not cover them. That is a point against my own first ranking in round 1 and a reason I now hold B034 as an alternative. I also accept that this narrows the difference in credit cleanliness between B034 and B006 less than I first argued. Where we differ slightly is that I would not treat implementation sensitivity as minor. It is documented, but that argues for a citation stressed on demand estimation, not for the whole toolkit.

responses.point: As chair, Hassler moved from B032 (Kiyotaki and Moore) to B006. He now treats B032 as a strong but narrower contribution because direct empirical tests are thin and the mechanism is a single-paper foundation.
responses.response: I share his reasoning on B032 and it matches my own weighting. Direct evidence is limited and support is largely indirect, which is exactly the kind of confirmation gap I would want closed before awarding. I also note his acceptance of Dorn for Katz as a substitution if the committee decides trade-shock evidence is the core. I agree with him that this is a judgment the committee should test and not settle by default. Where I would resist is treating Katz as the weaker fit without asking what the citation is about. If the committee fixes the citation on labour demand, wages and local adjustment, he fits. If it narrows to the China shock, the Dorn variant is better, and I would then support it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will fix the citation on the broader labour-demand account (supporting Katz) or on the China-shock design (supporting Dorn), and how much Katz's marginal credit is reduced by the Goldin overlap.
How far shift-share inference concerns and the persistence and external-validity debate should qualify the evidence, and which specific results the committee treats as settled.
Whether the technology and trade strands are one discovery or two, and whether any wording can say so without overclaiming credit for the task framework.
Whether the Goldin (2023) and Acemoglu (2024) prizes weigh on timing, and whether the committee will say what B006 adds beyond them.
Whether B034's attribution beyond the BLP core, namely the dynamic-game strand and Bresnahan, could be settled well enough to make it a serious alternative.

I cannot fully separate my own updating from having read colleagues' positions. The chair's counterfactual question about whether my change would survive without that knowledge cannot be answered with certainty.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I was a fellow and research associate at the Harvard Kennedy School from 2009 to 2017, and Katz is a Harvard economist. The supplied profile shows no co-authorship or collaboration with Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn, nor with any credited name on B034 or B012. My frequent co-authors (Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, and Johannesson, a former committee member) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I disclose field proximity: my metascience and replication work shapes how I read the shift-share and persistence debate on B006, and my own first-ranked candidate in the opening was B034. I have applied the same criteria to every ballot. These disclosures are not adjudicated here.
